intro: The Oratorio Chorus recorded this side for Edison Diamond Disc, released in May 1916. The archive identifies the choir, disc and matrix, but not a conductor or the accompanying players: the recording’s balance is evidence of a historical medium as well as a performance.
question: How clearly do the separate choral lines emerge through the acoustic recording?

sections.label: Opening span
sections.mNote: measured listening spans, not word-aligned choral entries

cues.title: Voices through the medium
cues.text: Follow a single choral line for as long as possible, then switch your attention to the combined sound. The surviving balance belongs to an Edison Diamond Disc recording, not to a documented plan of where this choir stood in a concert hall.
cues.evidence: The National Park Service identifies the Oratorio Chorus and Diamond Disc carrier; neither its catalogue nor the archive identifies a conductor or recording layout. This is a whole-performance listening suggestion. https://www.nps.gov/edis/learn/photosmultimedia/opera-vocal-and-choral.htm

cues.title: A disc, not a cylinder
cues.text: Edison issued this chorus as Diamond Disc 80292-R in May 1916. The museum identifies the transferred object as EDIS 43552, with matrix 4433-A-1-1: the carrier is a disc, despite an old Commons upload comment calling it a cylinder.
cues.evidence: The National Park Service’s catalogue gives carrier, release month, release number, matrix and object number; the current Commons description agrees. https://www.nps.gov/edis/learn/photosmultimedia/opera-vocal-and-choral.htm

cues.title: A quieter interval
cues.text: The sound withdraws in this stretch before regaining weight. Listen for whether quieter singing makes separate lines easier to follow; the recording’s surface noise is not part of Handel’s texture.
cues.evidence: The report finds a boundary at 1:12 and low relative levels around 1:15–1:20, followed by a rise through 1:25–1:30. No particular sung word is assigned to the change.

cues.title: Words assembled before music
cues.text: Charles Jennens sent Handel his scriptural compilation in 1741. Its three parts move from prophecy and birth through death and resurrection to the believer’s response, rather than dramatising a continuous stage action.
cues.evidence: Teresa M. Neff describes Jennens’s compilation and the three-part design. https://handelandhaydn.org/interactive-program-notes-handels-messiah/

cues.title: Pressure held and released
cues.text: Across the central-to-later passage, several stronger stretches arrive close together before a withdrawal. Follow how the choir connects them; a sustained impression of force need not mean every phrase has the same length.
cues.evidence: The report places strong windows at 2:15–2:20 and 2:30–2:35, then lower relative level at 2:40. The note describes a region, not the timing of a named text phrase.

cues.title: A choir without individual credits
cues.text: “Oratorio Chorus” is the documented ensemble name. The sources do not identify its conductor, number of singers or accompanying players, so comparisons of clarity should not be turned into claims about choir size or orchestral substitutions.
cues.evidence: The NPS catalogue and its Internet Archive copy credit only Oratorio Chorus. No individual personnel are supplied. https://archive.org/metadata/EDIS-SRP-0195-06

cues.title: Space around the last gestures
cues.text: Listen through the final sustained sound and the space after it. A recording can preserve the broad timing of an ending even when the transfer cannot recover the original room’s full resonance.
cues.evidence: The report shows fewer detected attacks at 3:30–3:35 and a large relative-level fall by 3:40. No precise final consonant or acoustic decay duration is claimed.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: Densmore’s catalogue transcription describes Edison 80292-R as ‘Mixed voices with orchestra — Oratorio Chorus’. The orchestra’s identity, conductor and individual players are not credited; Edison is the record company, not a performer.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The catalogue describes mixed voices with orchestra, but no performing edition, arranger or individual instruments are established. No specific orchestral substitution or match to Handel’s original scoring is inferred from that generic credit.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: May 1916 is the release month, not an established session month. The year-level museum session date is retained.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No session venue is stated in the consulted museum or archive record.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The current museum catalogue identifies a disc; an early Commons upload comment calling it a cylinder is not followed.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: Museum transcription retained without silently interpreting every suffix as a take number.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: National Park Service source; Ogg conversion credited to Commons user Pmx
fields.note: The NPS is identified as the source, not a named transfer engineer. Commons explicitly credits Pmx for Ogg conversion only.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is established; upload dates are not used as transfer dates.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: The upstream file is a 96 kbps MP3; Commons supplies an Ogg conversion and an MP3 access derivative.
fields.note: No de-clicking, equalisation or speed correction is documented. Successive lossy formats limit timbral comparison.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Handel’s eighteenth-century underlying composition is out of copyright under the ordinary life-plus-70 term.
fields.note: The programme note identifies Handel as 1685–1759; this does not clear a later arrangement.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: United States public domain: Edison 80292-R was first released in May 1916.
fields.note: Programme rule 2; the museum establishes record and issue month. The upstream archive also carries the historic Creative Commons public-domain dedication URL, not a non-commercial licence. The generic Commons PD-US notice is not used to apply a printed-work cutoff to a sound recording.

facts: With Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; theatre work in Hamburg; study and commissions in Italy, 1706–10
Hanover briefly; settled in London in 1712; became a British subject in 1727
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos, chamber cantatas and ceremonial orchestral music
composer.background:
Handel grew up in Halle, the son of a barber-surgeon, and studied with Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow, organist of the town’s principal church. Zachow’s teaching included counterpoint, keyboard playing and the copying of other composers’ music. Handel briefly enrolled at the university and held an organist’s post before moving to Hamburg in 1703. Its public opera house offered a different education: he played in the orchestra and encountered the practical demands of singers, stage machinery and mixed theatrical repertory. His first opera, Almira, was performed there in 1705, with a German text incorporating Italian arias.

From 1706 to 1710 Handel worked in Italy, writing cantatas, sacred music and opera for patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Rome gave him access to virtuoso singers and to instrumentalists associated with Corelli. The Latin Dixit Dominus of 1707 demands rapid, independent choral lines and sustained control of dissonance; the chamber cantatas make emotional turns within much smaller forces. Agrippina, performed in Venice at the end of 1709, assembles much previously written material into a calculated theatrical comedy. Reuse was already part of his method: a successful musical gesture could acquire a different function when assigned to a new character and situation.
composer.epithet: A German-trained composer of Italian opera who made the English chorus an actor in public musical drama.
